name: Kutai Malay / Bahasa Kutai
confidence_why: Suryadikara et al. 1979 state that Kutai Malay has no suprasegmental phonemes, Sugiyono 2007 repeats this and measures only phrase-final pitch peaks that van Heuven and van Zanten 2007 read as boundary tones rather than word accent, and no source gives a stress placement, so the record stays undetermined with nothing contradicting it.

KKB Bahasa Indonesia [mannok] 'ayam' [pattan] 'gelap' [pissan] 'pisang'" || Sugiyono 2007:160: "In the basic statement contour (cf. Figure 5) P1_pre coincided with the end of the /u/ of the pre-final syllable of the noun phrase sida busu ‘uncle’, whereas P1_peak coincided with the start of the final vowel /u/) of this noun phrase. ... In this syllable P2_pre was also situated, whereas P2_peak and P2_trail fell on the final syllable of this verb." || van Heuven & van Zanten 2007:195: "In Kutai Malay the pitch movement marking the boundary between subject and predicate in simple SV sentences seems to be much larger than the utterance-final accent-lending pitch movement."
sweep_summary: Language not in catalog. The single stress-titled item, Sugiyono 2003 (UI dissertation, 354 pp., Glottolog 59692), is about sentence prosody (declarative vs interrogative), not word stress; the dissertation itself is not open anywhere reachable (lib.ui.ac. Its English chapter version (Sugiyono 2007, LOT-OS9 ch.7, held by the project and read) states no word-stress rule; its only word-prosody remark (p.151) relays Suryadikara et al. 1979:10 that Kutai Malay has no suprasegmental phonemes, with some lengthening. Google Books snippets of the Indonesian precursor article (Sugiyono 2002, Bahasa dan Sastra 20(1)) likewise show no Kutai stress statement. Best available first-hand statement remains the Suryadikara 1979 'no suprasegmental phonemes' line (snippet-only) as relayed by Sugiyono 2007:151; acquiring the 2003 dissertation is medium priority (it may contain a fuller phonological background chapter, but its topic is intonation).

new_statements.translation: Suryadikara et al. 1979: '(d) Suprasegmental phonemes. Suprasegmental phonemes turn out not to be found in Bahasa Kutai. Although there is variation in how words are pronounced, that variation is not phonemic, so it is a matter of idiolect or local speech melody. For example the pronunciation difference between Kutai Tenggarong and Kutai Kota Bangun: KT [manok] [petan] [pisan] ... KKB [mannok] 'chicken' [pattan] 'dark' [pissan] 'banana'.'

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only located statement says suprasegmentals (stress/length/pitch) are not phonemic in Kutai Malay; no source seen states where word stress falls. The instrumental work (Sugiyono 2003/2007; van Heuven & van Zanten 2007:195) describes Tenggarong Kutai Malay prosody purely at phrase level: short phrases closed by boundary tones, pitch peaks realised on the phrase-final syllable(s) (e.g. on -su of 'sida busu', -cing of 'mancing'), and later handbook literature (Kaufman & Himmelmann 2020/2024) groups Kutai Malay with the Malay varieties analysed as lacking word stress -- but none of these says so explicitly for Kutai. Hence: stress non-contrastive, placement undescribed; the Leiden-school reading would be 'no word stress / phrase-final boundary prominence'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source seen.
new_statements.exceptions: Suryadikara et al. note non-phonemic pronunciation variation between the Tenggarong (KT) and Kota Bangun (KKB) varieties, KKB showing geminate medial consonants ([mannok], [pattan], [pissan]); Sugiyono adds 'indications that certain speech sounds are lengthened'.
new_statements.domain_note: Suryadikara: word-level phonemics (citation forms). Sugiyono / van Heuven & van Zanten: sentence prosody of read SV(O)(Adv) sentences; prominence described as phrase-boundary tones, with an 'utterance-final accent-lending pitch movement' smaller than the subject/predicate boundary movement.
new_statements.identity_note: Sugiyono 2003/2007 recorded 14 speakers who had lived in Tenggarong all their lives, i.e. Tenggarong Kutai Malay proper (teng1267, vkt). Suryadikara et al. 1979 'Bahasa Kutai (BK)' covers both the Tenggarong variety (BKT/KT) and the Kota Bangun variety (KKB = Kota Bangun Kutai Malay, kota1275, iso mqg); the geminate examples [mannok], [pattan], [pissan] are KKB. Collins 1992/2006 distinguishes 'Kutai Malay' (Tenggarong/downriver) from 'Kutai Lakes Malay' (Kota Bangun).

new_statements.quote: As regards prosody Suryadikara et al. (1979: 10) mention that there are no supra-segmental phonemes, although there are indications that certain speech sounds are lengthened.
new_statements.citation: Sugiyono. 2007. Prosodic markers of the statement-question contrast in Kutai Malay. In V.J. van Heuven & E. van Zanten (eds), Prosody in Indonesian Languages, 151-175. LOT Occasional Series 9. Utrecht: LOT. (English version of the 2003 UI dissertation)
new_statements.reading: Not a first-hand stress rule: Sugiyono relays Suryadikara et al. 1979 that Kutai Malay has no phonemic suprasegmentals (i.e., no contrastive word stress), noting only some segment lengthening. His own experimental work concerns sentence melody (statement vs. question), and the volume editors (van Heuven & van Zanten 2007:195) treat his Kutai pitch peaks as phrase-boundary tones larger than any utterance-final accent-lending movement. The 1979 primary (Suryadikara et al., Bahasa Kutai, p.10 '(d) Fonem Suprasegmental. Fonem suprasegmental ternyata tidak dijumpai dalam BK') is known only from Google Books snippets already held by the project. No source read in this search of works with stress in the title gives a positional word-stress rule for Tenggarong Kutai Malay.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

(1979: 10) mention that there are no suprasegmental phonemes, although there are indications that certain speech sounds are lengthened.' Body is an instrumental study (14 Tenggarong speakers) of statement vs question melody; pitch peaks sit on phrase-final syllables (P1_peak on final /u/ of 'sida busu', P2_peak on '-cing' of 'mancing', pp.160-161); no word-stress rule, the words stress/accent do not occur.
